current_anchors.current_text: \subsection{A benchmark-default validation protocol}\label{sec:v13-rp}

current_anchors.matched_text: 8 cases lose by over ten percent
current_anchors.current_text: The protocol combines the six-point menu in Table~\ref{tab:methods}, longer validation and a corrected-rank historical default. It selects the lowest mean validation loss over 156 weekly observations or 5,760 FX records. The selected candidate replaces historical headroom only when its paired validation improvement strictly exceeds one HAC standard error \citep{nw1987}. Across 60 weekly comparisons, the protocol retains historical headroom in 32 and has 0.00\% median excess, compared with 14.63\% for ordinary regression. This zero median reflects the majority of decisions retaining historical headroom. However, 8 cases lose by over ten percent, exceeding the prewritten five-percent ceiling for such cases; the worst excess is 80.98\% (Figure~\ref{fig:v13-rp}). Both FX periods retain the ordinary regression gains, meeting the criterion for retaining gains. The rule was designed after earlier findings and uses inspected evaluation periods, so this check is retrospective.

current_anchors.matched_text: This failed tail criterion limits
current_anchors.current_text: For RQ2, longer validation reduces full regression medians in both weekly reporting systems, but across-arm differences need not describe typical paired improvements (Table~\ref{tab:v13-validation}). These dealer aggregates remain related tasks, and the horizon-six New York Fed extension also moves the validation endpoint. The benchmark-default protocol cuts weekly median excess to 0.00\% and preserves FX gains, yet 8 of 60 cases still lose by over ten percent, with a worst excess of 80.98\% (Section~\ref{sec:v13-rp}). This failed tail criterion limits the protocol's risk-management recommendation, and the rejected high-quantile repair leaves its original judgments unresolved.

current_anchors.current_text: A fixed extension, committed locally before calculation and uploaded publicly afterward, examines the short-history pattern across 17 CFTC aggregate dealer-position markets. Its fixed horizon is six weeks. The 52- and 260-week results were already known and are reused unchanged; only the 520-week forecasts were new. current_anchors.matched_text: Longer validation improves full regression medians
current_anchors.current_text: \begin{abstract}Dealers monitor the largest absolute position reached before a review horizon ends. We compare conditional quantile models with historical rules on hourly foreign exchange (FX) positions, weekly New York Fed positions and Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) dealer positions, matching histories and update schedules. Historical rules are hard to beat. First, FX regression lowers matched loss by 14.8\% and 16.6\% in two periods, but its ranking against a shorter rolling rule changes. Second, in the initial weekly comparisons, historical headroom beats full regression in 34 of 48 New York Fed cases; the better realized historical score wins 29 of 34 CFTC cases. Longer validation improves full regression medians in both reporting systems; CFTC short-history excess falls from 19.3\% to 4.0\%. A benchmark-default gate retains FX gains and improves weekly median performance, but leaves large individual losses. Third, lower scores need not mean lower limit costs: higher reserve charges and lower fixed breach charges generally favor regression in CFTC. Costs are illustrative, and the evidence is retrospective; the original FX evaluation period had been inspected beforehand.\end{abstract}

Its median paired change is zero despite the lower long-validation arm median, so differences between arm medians need not represent typical improvements. The four-feature short-horizon New York Fed median-improvement screen fails. Its complete results and original CFTC failures remain available in Supplement Sections S36 and S38. current_anchors.matched_text: This gap describes the tested finite procedures
current_anchors.current_text: Loss from penalty selection exceeds half of positive actual excess loss in 27 of 41 short-history weekly comparisons (Figure~\ref{fig:v12-decomposition}). Extending validation lowers CFTC median excess loss from 19.33\% to 4.03\% with short histories, and from 10.35\% to 0.53\% with longer histories. The New York Fed medians fall from 6.68\% to -1.13\% at horizon six and from 40.47\% to 5.02\% at horizon twenty-four (Table~\ref{tab:v13-validation}). Yet the best finite penalty selected with evaluation hindsight still loses to historical headroom in 29 of 41 comparisons. This gap describes the tested finite procedures; it does not establish that conditional information is absent.

current_anchors.matched_text: The retrospective finite candidate uses five penalties
current_anchors.current_text: The decomposition separates the selected report's gap from the best finite candidate and that candidate's gap from historical headroom. The retrospective finite candidate uses five penalties and excludes the ordinary empirical limit, supplying a diagnostic rather than a deployable selection rule. Separate component medians need not add: actual excess is 19.44\%, selection 18.32\%, and the diagnostic gap 4.37\%. An empirical-limit selection can beat every finite candidate, making its selection component negative; both long-history FX horizons have negative finite-menu gaps.

current_anchors.matched_text: The nominal level presumes suitable loss dependence
current_anchors.current_text: We form a 90\% model confidence set separately for each complete source, period, horizon and history grid \citep{mcs2011}. The range statistic uses 1,000 stationary-bootstrap replications in arch 8.0.0, with block length $\max\{H,\lceil n^{1/3}\rceil\}$. All complete saved procedures enter on matching origin grids and targets, while incomplete prior methods remain explicitly unavailable. The nominal level presumes suitable loss dependence; it does not account for earlier research-stage model development.

current_anchors.matched_text: no independent cross-market pooled test
current_anchors.current_text: Exact duplicate loss columns enter the bootstrap once, and their procedure labels are restored afterward. Historical reports are merged only after their full forecasts and targets match, while rolling references remain distinct. Several methods can produce identical losses, so one surviving loss pattern need not mean that only one method survives. The fractions summarize related tasks, with no independent cross-market pooled test.

current_anchors.matched_text: Non-elimination establishes neither equal predictive risk
current_anchors.current_text: Matched historical methods remain in most confidence sets, usually alongside alternatives (Supplement Table~\vthirteenMCSTable{}). current_anchors.matched_text: the better realized historical score wins 29 of 34 CFTC cases
current_anchors.current_text: \begin{abstract}Dealers monitor the largest absolute position reached before a review horizon ends. We compare conditional quantile models with historical rules on hourly foreign exchange (FX) positions, weekly New York Fed positions and Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) dealer positions, matching histories and update schedules. Historical rules are hard to beat. First, FX regression lowers matched loss by 14.8\% and 16.6\% in two periods, but its ranking against a shorter rolling rule changes. Second, in the initial weekly comparisons, historical headroom beats full regression in 34 of 48 New York Fed cases; the better realized historical score wins 29 of 34 CFTC cases. Longer validation improves full regression medians in both reporting systems; CFTC short-history excess falls from 19.3\% to 4.0\%. A benchmark-default gate retains FX gains and improves weekly median performance, but leaves large individual losses. Third, lower scores need not mean lower limit costs: higher reserve charges and lower fixed breach charges generally favor regression in CFTC. Costs are illustrative, and the evidence is retrospective; the original FX evaluation period had been inspected beforehand.\end{abstract}

current_anchors.matched_text: rather than an executable selector
current_anchors.current_text: The independent reporting system gives a similar overall ranking: a historical headroom rule has lower loss in 29 of 34 contract/history comparisons. This meets the pre-specified 60\% threshold, using the better realized score of corrected and ordinary empirical historical reports rather than an executable selector. Corrected historical headroom remains the fixed matched reference, with the ordinary empirical version reported separately. Both full-regression medians exceed the pre-specified ten-percent tolerance, whereas four-feature regression moves closer to history with the longer window. These comparisons extend the benchmark pattern to a separate reporting system while retaining substantial contract-level variation (Table~\ref{tab:v10-cftc-contracts}; Figure~\ref{fig:v10-cftc}).

current_anchors.matched_text: Within the tested configurations
current_anchors.current_text: The fixed-period, short-horizon learning curve shows that more history helps only over part of the tested range (Figure~\ref{fig:v11-history}). Full regression moves from higher loss at the shortest history to its largest matched gain at an intermediate history. The gain is smaller at the longest history, while the four-feature curve changes sign within the tested range. Both curves use the original FX period and their original penalty menus; regression is compared with its own matched historical reference at each history length. Supplement Section S35 retains the full contrasts and synthetic confirmation summary. Within the tested configurations, the history and menu comparisons link conditional gains to history length and the availability of strong shrinkage.

current_anchors.matched_text: Full regression has no prewritten high-region cell
current_anchors.current_text: A fixed extension, committed locally before calculation and uploaded publicly afterward, examines the short-history pattern across 17 CFTC aggregate dealer-position markets. Its fixed horizon is six weeks. The 52- and 260-week results were already known and are reused unchanged; only the 520-week forecasts were new. Both prewritten low-history screens pass: QR4 loses to its matched rolling reference in 15 of 17 cells and QR33 in 29 of 34. The high-history QR4 screen fails, because 10 of 17 wins (58.8\%) fall below the fixed 60\% rule; strict improvement over all three windows holds in only 6 of 17 markets. Full regression has no prewritten high-region cell, leaving its high-history screen untestable. The primary verdict is therefore partial support. These dependent aggregate-market counts describe transport of a fixed prediction; they do not establish a generally sufficient financial history, a causal estimation-cost mechanism, or dealer-level replication. Supplement Section S39 gives all decision screens and counterexamples.
